newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Refugees pour out of Zaire, massacre victims found.
newsitem.headline: Refugees pour out of Zaire, massacre victims found.

text.p: As many as 700,000 Hutu refugees abandoned camps in east Zaire on Friday to trudge back to Rwanda, leaving behind mutilated corpses of a handful of men, women and children and a mystery as to how they died.
To the west, witnesses spoke of fighting between Zairean rebels and fleeing Hutu hardliners.

After night fell, heavy rain halted the human tide of refugees. Thousands huddled under plastic sheeting along the road to the east Zairean town of Goma from Mugunga, until Friday's exodus the world's largest refugee camp.
Over 100,000 refugees waited in Goma to cross the Rwandan border a few kilometres (miles) away on Saturday.

"It seems the whole pocket around Goma and Mugunga involving 700,000 plus people is on the move, most of them in this direction," U.N. refugee agency spokesman Ray Wilkinson told reporters in Goma earlier.
He said Mugunga was empty apart from rats and corpses.
"In one area near the Oxfam water tanks we discovered 26 dead people, all women and children apart from one man, macheted to death with their heads split open."
Reporters saw 13 more bodies in a ditch by the road to Goma. One woman had been decapitated and had her limbs cut off. She lay in a tangle of bodies and belongings.
Some refugees said Tutsi rebels had killed the refugees but this could not be independently confirmed. Others said Hutu hardliners had previously intimidated refugees into staying.

The exodus was made possible after an alliance of Zairean rebels, including ethnic Tutsis, drove back Rwandan Hutu militia and ex-government soldiers, breaking their stranglehold on refugees in the teeming wasteland of Mugunga.
Witnesses said fighting was continuing west of Mugunga as rebels pushed back Hutu militiamen, blamed for the genocide of up to a million minority Tutsis in Rwanda in 1994.

President Bill Clinton told a White House news conference the United States remained prepared to contribute troops to a Zaire relief mission despite the flow of Hutus back to Rwanda. "The world's most powerful nation must not turn its back on so many desperate people and so many innocent children," he said.

Washington announced this week it had agreed tentatively to send 1,000 troops to Goma to secure the airport and set up a protected corridor so refugees could return to Rwanda. About another 3,000 U.S. troops would provide support.
In New York, British U.N. envoy Sir John Weston said the Security Council agreed during closed-door consultations on a resolution to deploy a multinational force in eastern Zaire.
Hutu militia and Rwandan ex-government soldiers had made Mugunga camp a base in exile after fleeing to Zaire in 1994.
Zairean rebels bombarded the camp on Thursday, triggering the exodus.
"At this rate, most of these people could be home by the weekend, it is extraordinary we have seen the cracking of this problem in one day," Wilkinson said.
Rebels seized a strip of Zaire along its eastern border in a month of fighting against Zairean troops and Hutu hardliners.
"We all fled because of the fighting," said refugee Vincent Nzehsi. "I am going back to Rubavu, Rwanda. There are no militia in the camp, they are all in the forest."
The U.N.'s World Food Programme, waiting on the Rwandan side of the border with food, said up to 10,000 had already crossed with a further 275,000 backed up along the road.
Rwandan President Pasteur Bizimungu, himself a Hutu, went to the Gisenyi border post to welcome his fellow countrymen. He received a tumultuous reception from the refugees.
"We have come here to welcome the people to show them the whole population was waiting for them to reassure them there won't be any harassment. They are welcome in Rwanda," he said.
But underlining the volatile nature of the region, Zaire said it would wage war on Burundi and Rwanda which it accuses of violating its territory in fighting in its east.
"We are determined to wage a total war...We have the means," Zairean Deputy Foreign Minister Lokondo Yoka told a news conference in Brussels.
Zaire's ragged army is outnumbered by Rwanda's 54,000-strong force which is dominated by Tutsis who swept the then Hutu-led government from power in 1994 following the genocide.
